title: Wrong Patient
passages:
Ospina didn't wait to be asked. They dropped the hopper—a yard mule's big, dumb cousin, a low steel tray on six tires built to haul ballast and nothing cleverer—into gear and swung it broadside into the gap, filling it like a cork in a bottle.

The feral rig's nose sensor was still reading the world off the last good picture it had before the Blank swallowed its signal, and that picture now had four tons of parked hopper where open road used to be. It stopped dead, ten centimeters off the steel, brake lights on and staying on. It would sit there trusting a world that no longer existed until somebody handed it a new heading, and nobody was going to.

"Nice parking," Rhea said.

"I seal rigs, I don't park them," Ospina said. "Get your box up."

The mule coughed when Rhea keyed it. She'd pulled its drive relay and smashed the cab panel to kill the lockout, so she had steering back, but she had to hold the throttle wire against the post with her thumb, and the whole rig moved like a thing that resented being awake. The tow bar sat down at the lip of the culvert, the box tail hanging over the pipe, the sedated man rolling loose inside. She fed it power in threads, a few centimeters at a time, feeling for the moment the weight came off the tail and onto the road.

"Easy," Miko said, both palms flat on the box's rear doors like she could hold it up by wanting to. "Easy, easy—"

The tail came up. The tires bit gravel. All of it on solid ground now, mule and box and the man who wasn't on any manifest anyone would read.

Rhea took her thumb off the wire and the mule died again, and she sat there breathing.

Ospina was already turning the hopper's wheel, backing it out of the gap, and the moment it moved the feral rig crept forward half a meter and stopped behind the mule, obedient to a heading only it could see.

"Come with us," Rhea said. "We're blind out here. No transponder, no nav, no board. You've got the chipped stamp, you've got—"

"I've got a shift ending at oh-six-hundred and a door that reads my badge every time I walk through it." Ospina held up the stamp, the one with the corner chipped out, and Rhea saw for the first time that it wasn't Ospina's hand that had done the resealing—Ospina held it the way you hold something you found. "This plate your loader jammed in the track." They tipped their head at the hinge still wedged in the door. "Not Bay 4 stock. I sign out every plate we run and I never signed that one out. Somebody walked it into my yard tonight, and it wasn't me."

"Then help me—"

"Then I've got a long dark between me and a clean board, and if I'm not standing at that door at six, the next thing I seal is my own cell." Ospina swung the hopper around, pointed it back toward Kettering, toward whatever waited there with a chipped stamp and a manifest built out of lies. "Forty klicks to Anza. You did thirty before you met me. Do the rest."

And they were gone, taillights shrinking into the Blank.

Miko looked at Rhea. Rhea looked east.

"Forty klicks," she said. "Blind. In a rig that can't shout its own number." Somewhere past the end of that road Ivo was under a cracked diaphragm, breathing for both of them on borrowed parts, and every one of these kilometers was one he didn't have.

She thumbed the wire. The mule woke up angry.

"Then let's not tell it its number," Miko said, climbing into the passenger side. "Let's just drive."

Rhea drove. Dead signal, a box that logged no one, and a passenger she trusted less than the truck—and at the far end, her brother counting down every kilometer she hadn't covered yet.

The Blank ran east in a shallow trough of old riverbed, and the mule took it at forty because Rhea wouldn't give it more. Over forty the washboard shook the throttle wire out from under her thumb, and then they were cargo like the box behind them.

Miko rode with her boots on the dash and the repeater turned toward her—the pod's own four-line screen, copied forward on a wire so the driver can read it without climbing out into the weather.

"Passenger core temperature stable," she said. "Thirty-six point four."

"Good."

"Thirty-six point four."

"I heard you the first time."

"It's been thirty-six point four since Kettering." Miko tapped the glass. "It's a nice number. I'd like a different one."

Rhea kept her thumb down and thought about it, because a man under sedation does not hold a number. The heater cycles, the pump in the mattress pad kicks, the box breathes: thirty-six two, thirty-six six, thirty-six three. She'd sat with a hundred of these screens on rigs she had no business touching.

She also knew what the box did when its databus died—the cable bundle that carries the sensor readings up to the screen. It didn't blank. It held the last page it had read. Last good picture. Same as the feral rig back there, stopped dead on a road that had moved.

There was a clamp meter in the door pocket, tongs that close around a cable and read the current running through it without cutting anything. She leaned, clamped it on the pod's cell lead, and watched the digits settle.

One point two amps. A sedated hundred-kilo man, a heater, and a mattress pump should have been pulling five or six.

She put her palm over the box's exhaust vent and held it there long enough to be sure. Cold. No heat coming out of a box that was supposedly holding a man at thirty-six point four.

"See," Miko said. "Dead."

"Cold isn't dead." Rhea dropped the meter back in the pocket. "The box is dead. That's a different problem."

"Is it? Because from in here they look like the same problem with better manners."

Ahead, low on the horizon, the sky had a stain on it: sodium light, Anza's main gate, where the reader shouts every rig's number out to the board and the board writes it down. Except this rig had no transponder to shout with, which meant it would arrive as nothing at all, and a nothing at a gate is worse than a number.

"Left at the leaning post," Miko said.

Rhea took the left. Two hundred meters on, Miko said, "Right. Slow."

"There's no road here."

"There's a siding." Miko pointed with two fingers, like she was calling a card. "Freight spur. Ore hoppers loaded there back when anybody shipped ore. The gate never reads it because there's nothing on it to read."

Rhea pulled the wire up a thread and let the mule roll, and looked at her. "You've driven this."

"I've never driven anything in my life. I load it."

"Then how do you know where the ore siding is."

Miko was quiet for three posts. Then she said, "Because I've been walking it since Kettering. Not this stretch, the maps of it. I counted the reflectors off a hopper seat on a night shift nobody was watching, and I know there's a stub of dead road in the dark on the east side of Anza, and I know what leaves from it at oh-four-hundred." She shrugged. "Three tickets to the coast, three names, all paid. If I roll through that lit gate tonight I'm a body on a board, and the exit I bought burns with me."

"You could have said that in the yard."

"You'd have put me off the mule."

"I still might."

"You won't. You need somebody who knows where the dark is." Miko grinned at her, entirely too pleased. "Also I'm fun."

Rhea did the arithmetic she'd been doing for an hour, the only arithmetic that mattered: forty klicks at forty, and an hour of Ivo breathing through a cracked diaphragm at the far end of it, waiting on a sister who was driving a truck with her thumb.

The siding came up on the right, black gravel, no light on any of it.

She took her thumb off the wire and the mule died, and in the quiet she climbed down and walked back along the box with the meter still in her fist. Thirty-six point four, on a screen that hadn't read the man once all night.

She put her hand flat on the pod lid.

It was warm. Not machine-warm. Warm like a person.

The lid was warm under her palm, and the mule was dead, and for a couple of seconds Rhea stood in the dark with her hand on a man she'd spent forty kilometers believing was a number on a screen.

Then the yard light came on.

One sodium lamp on a bent pole at the end of the stub, buzzing up from nothing to orange, and under it a man in a relay operator's coveralls with a hand lamp—a rubber torch you carry when the mast lights are out and you don't trust your own feet.

"Kill that," Rhea said.

He killed it. Then he came on anyway, unhurried, the way a man walks when the ground is his.

"You're on Anza ore siding," he said. "I'm Teodoro, I run the relay here, and I've been on the board since twenty-two hundred, which means I know things. Anza didn't file a medical handoff tonight. Not one. A handoff is the other end saying *send him, I'm ready, I've got the bay warm*—and nobody said it. No inbound medical, no outbound, no pod, nothing." He rapped the box's flank with his knuckles. "This isn't on my board. It isn't on any board. It's a Kettering ghost with a Kettering yard on the side of it, and nobody in this node is expecting a patient."

"There's a man in it," Rhea said.

"There's a man in a lot of things. There's a coast hopper string comes through this stub at oh-four-hundred, for instance, and I don't know why I said that."

"Don't," Miko said, from the far side of the mule, where she had arranged herself into a shape that was mostly shadow.

"Don't what?"

"Don't *finish* anything. You're a talker. I've met talkers."

Rhea took her hand off the lid and put it back on, because the warmth was the only reading tonight that hadn't lied to her. "The pod screen says thirty-six point four, steady, all the way from Kettering."

"Which screen?"

"The repeater. On a wire, off the pod."

Teodoro made a small noise, the kind you make at a child carrying a full cup. "Databus is cut, or that screen would be arguing with itself. Last good page. It'll hold thirty-six point four till the sun comes up." He tipped the lamp toward the box's belly without switching it on. "What's the cell pulling?"

"One point two amps."

"Then it's cold and it's holding a picture of a warm man." He scratched his jaw. "Also your brother's in my shop on the yard bottle, and I taped his diaphragm, and it holds as long as he doesn't argue with it. Four hours of bottle. Maybe five if I turn the shop heater down, which I have."

Rhea stood very still with her thumb near the throttle wire. "You could have led with that."

"You could have led with why you're parked on my siding with a rig that can't shout its own number." He said it without heat, and then he laughed once. "Ah. There it is. Never mind, I don't want it."

"I want to know who's in the box."

"Everybody wants to know that. It's the only interesting question on this continent tonight." He came around to the rear doors and crouched, and ran two fingers under the lip of the lid where the seal sat in its channel—Bay 4 stock, four bolts, a chipped stamp's ghost still visible in the wax. "Pod's got a manual release here. Under the lip. You pull it, the lid comes up on the strut, and the pod logs an open."

"Logs it to who? It's got no databus."

"To nobody. That's the mercy of it." He looked up. "But it breaks the seal. Once it's open it's never sealed again, and I've spent eleven years in this yard learning not to break a seal I can't re-stamp. I don't have a stamp. I don't have a plate. I've got a hole in my stock I can't explain to a man at oh-six-hundred."

"Then don't touch it," Rhea said. "I'll touch it."

She got her fingers under the lip. The wax was soft. It had been warm for a while.

From inside the box, three times, something knocked.

PASSAGE ends.

She had two fingers under the lip and the steel finger-loop of the manual release against her knuckle, and the knocking came again. Three times. Patient, spaced, the way you knock on a door you aren't sure anybody's behind.

"He's got rhythm," Teodoro said. "No rhythm is the bad one."

Rhea pulled the loop. Something let go inside with a sound like a jar lid giving, and the lid came up on its strut—the gas arm that holds a hatch so you don't have to—and the cold that had been sitting in that box all night rolled out over her boots.

He was big. That was the first thing, big through the shoulders in a way no sick man gets to be, coveralls unzipped to the sternum, one forearm thrown across his eyes against a light that wasn't on. The second thing was that he was breathing deep and even, like a man doing a job. The third thing was his hands.

She took the left one and turned it over in the lamp spill. Black crescents under every nail, ground in past the quick. You get that out of a fifth-wheel jaw or a packing gland. You do not get it at a desk, and you do not get it in a med bay.

"You're a loader," she said.

"I'm—" His mouth worked on it and gave up. "Ask me in an hour."

"The drug takes your name first and hands it back last," Teodoro said. "He'll be fine. He'll be extremely annoying."

"Water," the man said.

Rhea got the bottle out of the mule's door pocket and gave it to him, and he drank half of it sitting up with his back against the pod's inner wall, wincing, working one shoulder in a slow circle.

"There's a bracket in this box," he said. "Somebody's left a *bracket* in here, under my hip, for—" He stopped, blinking at the dark like he was counting something and losing. "How long have I been in there."

"Five hours, give or take," Teodoro said. "You missed your shift."

"I don't miss shifts."

"Cold isn't dead," Miko said, from the far side of the mule.

"Don't," Rhea said.

She tipped the lid back to look at the underside, and there was the card, in a wire holder, the way a chit rides in a holder so the next crew knows what they're carrying without opening anything. She pulled it out and turned it to the yard light.

A name. A badge number. And under it, in the flat type of a Kettering med printer: *LOGGED OUT 21:47. DISCHARGED.*

"Four and a half hours ago he walked out of Kettering med on his own legs," she said. "And then somebody put him in an empty box."

"Ballast," Teodoro said, and when she looked at him he shrugged. "Weight. Dead load you carry so a rig tracks straight on a crosswind. A box logged ballast is a box nobody at the far end opens, because ballast doesn't get delivered anywhere. It just arrives."

"So nobody's expecting a patient."

"Nobody's expecting anything. I told you. This rig's a ghost."

Rhea stood there with the card in her fist and did the arithmetic she'd been doing since Kettering, except now the sum came out different. Forty kilometers. A smashed cab panel. Her thumb on a bare wire for an hour and ten. Ivo on a yard bottle at the far end of it with his diaphragm taped, four hours of air, maybe five. All of it spent towing a readout.

"I drove forty klicks for a screen," she said.

"You drove forty klicks for a man," Teodoro said. "The screen just lied about which."

The man in the box drank the rest of the water. When he lowered the bottle his eyes had come back into focus, and he looked at Rhea, and then past her at the black gravel and the dead pole and the coast string's stub of road going off into nothing.

"Okay," he said. "Okay. Last thing I remember proper." He rubbed his jaw with the back of a filthy hand. "Bay four. End of shift, I'm clocking my seal bar back in and there's a loader out on the pad doing the four rigs, one after another, whole row, like he's got all night. Wax, stamp, wax, stamp." He held up his own hand and worked an imaginary stamp down twice. "And he's got a stamp with the corner chipped out of it. Little triangle gone out of the edge."

Teodoro had gone very quiet, which for Teodoro took effort.

"He kept looking at me while he did it," the man said. "That's the part I keep getting. Not at the rigs. At me. And then the lid came down, and that was his face, going away in the gap."

Nobody moved. The yard light buzzed, the mule ticked as it cooled, and every face on that siding turned to the far side of the box, where the shadow was.

"Come round where he can see you," Rhea said.

"I can see fine."

"He's got a drug in him and his memory coming back in pieces. He's not going to be polite about it."

Miko came around the mule's nose with her hands out of her pockets, and the man in the pod looked at her for a long moment, the way you look at a load you're not sure is strapped.

"You're not him," he said. "The loader."

"No."

"You were in the wall."

"Tool void," Miko said. "Gap between the box's inner skin and the frame, where the air lines run. Wide as a coffin and twice as warm. I've been in it since Kettering yard. Since before you went in." She tipped her chin at the box. "You came in on the forks. Somebody counted to three and let go, and you landed on the bracket, and I heard your shoulder go."

Teodoro raised the hand lamp an inch. "That's a long time in a wall."

"It's a long winter everywhere else."

Rhea turned the manifest card over in her fist, the one that said *DISCHARGED 21:47*, and then she looked at the plate still wedged in the door track, steel with wax in the bend of it. "Bay 4's seal authority caught up with us in the Blank. They took one look at that plate and said it isn't Bay 4 stock, and nobody signed it out of their crib tonight."

"It isn't out of any crib," Miko said. "It was in the void when I got in. Wedged behind the air line with wax in the bend, same as that." She shrugged. "It's the only steel in there. When your box started sealing itself I needed something to put in the track. So I used the thing somebody left me."

"Somebody left you a hinge plate in a wall," Teodoro said.

"Somebody left a lot of things in a lot of walls. I'm not going to be the one who says which." Miko's voice stayed flat and that was worse than shouting. "A witness gets a badge read. A badge read gets a board line. A board line has my face on it, and then the three tickets I paid for are three pieces of paper, and winter's in eleven weeks."

"Three names," Rhea said.

"Three names, three fares, one coast. Paid in full at Kettering, and every one of them dies the second somebody at Anza writes me down."

Rhea had spent the whole night reading instruments. Amp draw, core temperature, a card in a wire holder that swore a man had walked out of med on his own legs. Every one of them had lied to her in a calm voice. The instrument standing in front of her now had grease under its nails and had told her about the ore siding two kilometers before the ore siding existed.

"Teodoro," she said. "She rode in on the axle."

"The axle isn't a person."

"Then log the axle." Rhea put the card in her coverall pocket. "She's not cargo, she's not on my manifest, and I'm not writing her into your board at shift change so your oh-six-hundred can have something to chew."

Teodoro looked at the open box, at the seal channel with its clean broken wax, and rubbed the back of his neck. "Fine. But that box can't be sitting on my stub at six with its lid up and its seal cut. So everybody who isn't a box goes now."

Miko was already moving. She stopped at the front of the mule, one hand on the hot flank of it.

"Your brother's the one in the shop with the light over the door," she said. "Tell him his sister drives like a loader."

"Go on."

"I'm fun, though."

"Walk."

She went up the stub, past the dead pole, into the dark where the coast string's road ran, and she didn't look back, which Rhea respected and would not have said out loud.

The man in the pod watched the dark a while after she'd gone. Then he said, "There was a second one."

Rhea turned. "At the pad?"

"At the box. Holding the lid up while the other one stamped. I never saw a face, I had my eyes shut, I was busy being sick." He worked his shoulder in its slow circle. "But I heard him. He was counting."

"Counting what?"

"Down." The man's eyes came up, and they were steady now, and unhappy. "Out loud. Five. Four. Three."

Nobody said anything. Rhea looked at the open lid on its strut, at the door track where a stolen plate had held the bay open long enough for a man to keep breathing, and Teodoro said, very quietly, "Then whoever loaded him knew what that box does when it loses its signal."

PASSAGE ends.

Teodoro kept going—whoever loaded the box had known the box, known that a cut databus holds its last good picture, known a cold man reads as a warm number all the way across the Blank—and Rhea let it run over her, because she'd stopped trusting readouts tonight and started trusting the weight of a warm lid under her hand.

"Your loader can sweat it out on my couch," Teodoro said, winding down at last. "Shoulder wants a splint, I've got tape and opinions. Your brother's the one who can't wait, and he's been not-waiting four hours."

Rhea was already walking.

The Anza shop was a long shed that smelled of hot metal and old coffee, one bay lit and the rest parked full of dead rigs in pieces. She backed the mule's nose through the door, killed it, and unbolted the transponder off the dash—the broadcast box that shouts a rig's number out to the board so the board can write it down—and set the ruined thing on the bench. A to-do. The night already had too many.

Ivo was under the bay light on a rolling stool, gray around the mouth, a mask over his face and a yard bottle of air hissing at his shoulder. The pump beside him was breathing for him—a bellows, a rubber diaphragm inside it flexing to shove each breath in—and the diaphragm had a crack in it you could hear, a thin whistle of air going where it shouldn't.

"Taped it," Teodoro said from the door. "Holds if he stays calm."

"He's my brother," Rhea said. "He's never been calm."

Ivo's eyes opened. He dragged the mask down an inch to talk, which the pump hated.

"You drove a truck."

"I drove a truck."

"With your thumb?"

"Word travels."

"It does not," he said, and put the mask back, which was as near to laughing as a cracked diaphragm lets you get.

She had him off the stool and flat on the creeper—the wheeled board you lie on to slide under a rig—and the pump housing open in ninety seconds: four screws, a ring, and the cracked disc coming out in two tired pieces. She went through the scrap drawer fast and sure and came up with a square of heavy glove rubber, the thick palm kind that doesn't care about heat. Cut a disc against the old one for size, seated it, ran the screws down even so it wouldn't pinch, and worked the pump by thumb. Clean air. No whistle.

"Try it."

Ivo breathed. The mask fogged and cleared. His lips came up off gray into a color a person could live behind.

"Where'd you learn that."

"Same place you learned to load. Somebody showed me once and I didn't forget it."

She stayed. There was no version of the night where she didn't. She set the yard bottle to recharge, wiped her hands, picked up a wrench because her hands wanted work, and started in on the dead transponder—because it was broken, and she was here, and her brother was pulling his own air an arm's length away.

Two hundred klicks west, at the Kettering night board, Kass had a headset on, a coffee gone cold, and badge 2241 sitting on the master channel where it would sit forever now, logged, a door that wouldn't shut. Four ghost rigs. They'd held four since twenty-two hundred, four numbers peeled off the schedule one by one, and Kass had them stacked in a column on the wall screen, waiting to see what shape they made.

At 04:51, one of the four went.

Number, time, node—all of it lifting off the board while Kass watched, the way a name lifts off a manifest. No alarm. No scrub line. Just gone, clean, like it had never been routed at all.

"Somebody's tidying up," Kass said, to the headset, to the master, to the badge.

The channel gave back the flat nothing of the Blank.

And somewhere east of Anza, in a yard with a hole in its seal stock it couldn't explain, a stamp with a triangle chipped out of one corner sat in the dark, waiting for the next hand that would swear it had only found it.
